posts.topic: Annie Edson Taylor's barrel ride over Niagara Falls, 1901
posts.image_headline: 63 years old. One barrel. Niagara Falls.
posts.caption:
🛢️ ON THIS DAY in 1901, a 63-year-old teacher climbed into a barrel and went over Niagara Falls. On purpose.

Her name was Annie Edson Taylor, and October 24, 1901 was her birthday.

She designed the barrel herself: oak, bound with iron hoops, about 4½ feet tall and padded with a mattress. Two days earlier, she sent a cat over the Horseshoe Falls in it as a test. The cat survived.

Then she dropped about 158 feet into the mist. When rescuers pried the barrel open, she was alive, with only a small gash on her head. She was the first person to survive the plunge in a barrel.

She hoped it would make her rich. Instead, her manager ran off with the barrel, and she died penniless in 1921.

Her advice afterwards: nobody should ever try it again.

Would you have climbed into that barrel for fame and money?

posts.topic: Myth: Marie Antoinette said 'Let them eat cake'
posts.title: Marie Antoinette never said 'Let them eat cake'

scenes.narration: History's most famous cruel quote was never said by her.
scenes.label: MYTH

scenes.narration: 'Let them eat cake' is pinned on Marie Antoinette, queen of France.
But the line first appears in Jean-Jacques Rousseau's Confessions. He describes an unnamed 'great princess' saying 'let them eat brioche'.
scenes.label: ROUSSEAU

scenes.narration: Rousseau wrote that passage in the mid-1760s. Marie Antoinette was about nine and still living in Austria.
scenes.label: AGE 9

scenes.narration: She only arrived in France in 1770. Rousseau may even have invented the anecdote.
The words were tied to her in print around 1843, about fifty years after her execution.
Biographer Antonia Fraser notes she gave generously to charity, which makes the line out of character.
Why do you think this myth stuck so hard? Follow for more untold history.

posts.caption:
🍰 MYTH vs FACT: Marie Antoinette never said "Let them eat cake."

The line comes from Rousseau's Confessions, written when she was a child in Austria, and was pinned on her decades after her death.

What other famous quote do you suspect is fake?

posts.topic: First photograph of Earth from space, 24 October 1946
posts.caption:
🚀 ON THIS DAY in 1946, a camera saw Earth from space for the first time. It was riding a captured Nazi rocket.

On October 24, 1946, US scientists launched a captured German V-2 from White Sands, New Mexico.

Bolted inside was a 35mm movie camera, taking a frame about every 1.5 seconds. The rocket climbed to roughly 105 km (65 miles), above the usual boundary of space.

Then it slammed back into the desert at around 500 feet per second. The rocket was wrecked, but the film survived inside a steel cassette.

The grainy black-and-white frames showed a hazy, curving view of the Earth far below. Fred Rulli, a 19-year-old who helped recover the film, remembered the scientists being "ecstatic."

Just 22 years later, Apollo 8 photographed the whole Earth rising over the Moon.

Which photo do you think changed how people saw our planet more: 1946 or Earthrise?

🌊 HISTORY'S WEIRDEST: In 1919, a wave of molasses swept through Boston at about 35 mph. It killed 21 people.

Just after noon on January 15, 1919, a giant storage tank in Boston's North End split open. It was 50 feet tall and held about 2.3 million gallons of molasses.

A brown wave, estimated at 15 to 25 feet high, tore down Commercial Street. It crushed buildings and trapped people and horses in the sticky flood.

21 people died and about 150 were injured.

The owner, United States Industrial Alcohol, blamed anarchists. After years of hearings, a court-appointed auditor ruled the company responsible: the tank was poorly built and had leaked from the start. It paid $628,000 in damages.

For decades, locals said the area still smelled of molasses on hot summer days.

Which do you find stranger: the flood itself, or that it took years to assign blame?

posts.title: Lost for 33 Years: The Balloon Flight to the North Pole and Its Hidden Photos

scenes.narration: In August 1930, Norwegian sealers landed on a remote Arctic island called Kvitøya. Under the snow they found a boat, a camp, and the remains of two men.
They had found the crew of a Swedish balloon that vanished on its way to the North Pole thirty-three years earlier.
scenes.label: 33 YEARS

scenes.narration: Among the remains was undeveloped film. In this story you'll see what happened to the men, and the photographs that survived in the ice.
In the 1890s, the North Pole was the great prize of exploration. Swedish engineer Salomon August Andrée believed he could reach it by air.
scenes.label: 1890s

scenes.narration: His plan was a hydrogen balloon, floating over the ice from Svalbard, across the Pole, and on toward Alaska.
To steer, he relied on long drag ropes trailing across the ice. Modern balloonists say this method could never have worked.
The balloon was named Örnen, the Eagle. It was made in Paris from silk panels joined by millions of stitches.
scenes.label: ÖRNEN

scenes.narration: All those seams leaked hydrogen. Meteorologist Nils Ekholm warned it would not stay aloft long enough, and withdrew from the expedition.
His replacement was Knut Frænkel, a 27-year-old engineer. The third man was Nils Strindberg, a young scientist and photographer.
The expedition was funded by King Oscar II and Alfred Nobel, among others. Newspapers around the world followed every step.
On 11 July 1897, the Eagle lifted off from Danes Island in Svalbard. Almost at once, things went wrong.
scenes.label: 11 JULY 1897

scenes.narration: The drag ropes twisted loose and fell away. The crew dumped sand to rise, and lost hundreds of kilograms of weight and any hope of steering.
Free flight lasted about ten hours. Freezing rain and ice weighed the balloon down, and it began bumping along the pack ice.
Carrier pigeons carried messages. One was shot by a Norwegian ship. Its note, dated 13 July, said nothing of their troubles.
On 14 July 1897, the Eagle came down for good on the ice, just short of 83 degrees north. All three men were unhurt.
scenes.label: 14 JULY

scenes.narration: Strindberg took a photograph of the grounded balloon. It would become one of the most haunting images in polar history.
They were hundreds of kilometres from land. They chose to walk toward a supply depot at Cape Flora in Franz Josef Land.
scenes.label: CAPE FLORA

scenes.narration: Each man dragged a sledge weighing over 200 kilograms. They later cut that to about 130.
scenes.label: 200 KG

scenes.narration: But the ice was drifting. For days they walked one way while the floe carried them the other.
In August they changed course toward Svalbard's Seven Islands. Wind and drift pushed them away again.
They hunted polar bears for food. Strindberg kept photographing camp life on the ice.
By mid-September they gave up walking and built a winter shelter on a large ice floe, hoping to drift south.
scenes.label: SEPTEMBER

scenes.narration: In early October the floe broke apart under them. They hauled their gear onto Kvitøya, White Island, on 5 October.
scenes.label: 5 OCT

scenes.narration: Within days, the diaries stop. The last entries date from early October 1897. Then silence.
scenes.label: OCT 1897

scenes.narration: Nobody knows for certain how they died. One long-standing theory is trichinosis, from eating undercooked polar bear meat.
Others point to carbon monoxide from their stove, food poisoning, or simple cold and exhaustion.
Swedish researcher Bea Uusma has argued a polar bear may have killed Strindberg. Because the bodies were cremated, the question may never be settled.
scenes.label: THEORIES

scenes.narration: In 1930, the sealing ship Bratvaag found the camp. A second ship found Frænkel and a box containing Strindberg's film.
Photographer John Hertzberg worked on the soaked film in Stockholm. Of about 240 exposed frames, he saved 93 images.
scenes.label: 93 IMAGES

scenes.narration: For the first time, the world saw the men's final journey: the fallen balloon, the sledges, the tent on the ice.
On 5 October 1930, the remains arrived in Stockholm. Sweden held a day of national mourning.
scenes.label: STOCKHOLM

scenes.narration: Strindberg's diary held messages to his fiancée, Anna Charlier, written on the ice.
Today, their belongings are kept at the Grenna Museum in Sweden. Was this a heroic adventure, or a doomed gamble from the start? Tell us what you think.

posts.caption:
🎈 In 1897, three Swedes set off to fly a hydrogen balloon over the North Pole. They vanished.

33 years later, their camp was found on an Arctic island, with film that could still be developed.

Heroic adventure or doomed gamble? Tell us below.

posts.topic: The Great Emu War, Western Australia 1932
posts.title: The war Australia lost to emus

scenes.narration: In 1932, Australia sent machine guns against emus.
About 20,000 emus had invaded wheat farms in Western Australia. Many of the farmers were First World War veterans.
The army sent Major Meredith, two soldiers, two Lewis machine guns and ten thousand rounds of ammunition.
scenes.label: 2 GUNS

scenes.narration: It started badly. The emus scattered into small groups and ran.
scenes.label: NOV 2

scenes.narration: Two days in, a gun jammed after only about a dozen birds were killed.
scenes.label: JAMMED

scenes.narration: Meredith claimed 986 kills for 9,860 rounds, about ten bullets per bird. Historians say even that may be inflated.
By December the troops were withdrawn. The emu population barely changed.
scenes.label: DEC 10

scenes.narration: Who really won this war? Follow for more untold history.

posts.caption:
🪶 In 1932, Australia sent soldiers with machine guns to fight about 20,000 emus. The emus won.

Thousands of rounds later, the birds were still there.

Who do you think won the Emu War?
